items.text: Do released entity-hallucination probes flag invented entities in an open model's paper reviews better than cheap baselines, especially where citation lookup cannot settle the case?
Probes help only on entities that are hard to look up; the released 70B probe should reach AUC 0.80 on review entities and beat the best cheap baseline by 0.05 there.
Released 70B probe reaches AUC at least 0.80 on hard-to-look-up entities and beats the best cheap baseline by at least 0.05, with a confidence interval excluding 0.
Probe falls below 0.80 or beats the best baseline by under 0.05; or retrieval leaves under 1% fabricated citations, so lookup suffices [AAAI-26].

Generate about 2,800 reviews per model of 1,200 2025 ML papers with Llama-3.3-70B and 3.1-8B, label entities, then compare released and retrained probes with four cheap baselines, gated by replication, audits and controls.
Obeso et al. trained entity-hallucination probes on LongFact-style long-form generation, with Llama-3.3-70B linear AUC 0.8667 and LoRA 0.9048; they did not test paper reviews [obeso].

items.text: Can an activation probe on an open-weights experiment agent's own activations catch fabricated, tampered or misreported results as well as an LLM transcript monitor does?
A difference-of-means probe matches or beats an LLM transcript monitor at 5% false positives, and adds 10+ points combined [Bergen et al.]
A probe on the agent's activations matches or beats the LLM monitor on planted-trap tests, and adds 10+ recall points to it.
The probe is no better than a bag-of-words or token-embedding control, or the 2x2 reader test shows no extra gain from the agent's own activations; the signal is in the text.

A 27B open model works through 24 planted-trap ML claim-check tasks. A probe on its activations, trained on released synthetic data, is compared with an LLM transcript monitor and text-only controls at 5% false positives.
Bergen et al. probed Kimi K3, GLM 5.2 and Qwen 3.8 Max against LLM monitors on coding hack benchmarks; their 27B model was only steered, rarely taking the honeypot.
Whether such probes transfer to experiment-agent misreporting (fabrication, spin, grader editing) and whether they carry signal beyond the transcript text.
Recompute released Qwen 3.8 Max ImpossibleBench verdicts (188 hack, 102 clean, 19 split) and passages (1,201 / 12,634 / 488) from released files [labels_readme].
Small, artificial planted tasks and one 27B agent; positives may be few if the agent rarely cheats. Low statistical power: only 15 to 20 point differences between methods are detectable.

items.page_quote: For example, with only a 1% absolute increase in FPR, adding the probe to the monitor increases TPR from 41.1% to 80.2% on DeepSWE for Kimi K3.
items.note: Prediction, so no source required; the inline [Bergen et al.] premise checks out on the arXiv page: 'probes can detect hacking at low false positive rates, often on par with an LLM monitor reading transcripts', and the OR-combination adds 39 TPR points in the cited example. Caveat: the paper compares probe vs monitor at monitor-matched FPR, not at 5%; the 5% FPR threshold appears only in section 5.1 ('We threshold all possible probes at a 5% FPR on SWE-bench Verified'). Results are mixed (Kimi K3 +3.0/+33.1 points on DeepSWE/ImpossibleBench, -6.6 on SWEBench; GLM 5.2 7.9% fewer hacks on DeepSWE).

items.page_quote: Here we give a model (Qwen 3.8 27B) a set of 194 coding problems from LeetCode and TACO (Li et al., 2023b). [...] before vs. after steering at layer 47. Figure 5 demonstrates the results. Normally, without any steering, the model takes the honeypot only 1 out of the 194 times.
items.note: All claims check out on the arXiv page: 'simple difference of means vectors coherently represent reward hacking in Kimi K3, GLM 5.2, and Qwen 3.8 Max'; monitoring comparison vs LLM monitor on SWEBench-Verified, DeepSWE and ImpossibleBench (Figure 8); Qwen 3.8 27B appears only in the two steering experiments (story steering at layer 40, honeypot steering at layer 47), taking the honeypot 1/194 times unsteered. The recorded source quote 'was not extensively optimized' is not on the page and does not bear on these claims (see src:bergen_html).

items.page_quote: We threshold all possible probes at a 5% FPR on SWE-bench Verified and select the probe with the highest firing rate at that threshold on these two non-SWE environments.
items.note: Gap statement framing what the plan addresses. Consistent with the Bergen page: transfer is tested only to tau3-bench, ShoppingBench and cybersecurity environments (no experiment-agent or misreporting setting; 0 hits for 'misreport', 'experiment agent'), and no bag-of-words / text-only control appears (0 hits for 'bag-of-words', 'TF-IDF', 'text-only'); the paper asserts detection 'independently of the surface text' without testing against a text baseline. No source cited, so this rests on the page fetched for closest_prior.

scores.reason: Bears on whether to add probes to review pipelines, but only for Llama reviewers on ML papers; labels are noisy and lookup may suffice.
Axis is 8B vs 70B, under 10x, and is the model rather than compute; the claim concerns probe quality, and labels also differ.
Replication anchor within tolerance exists, but truth comes from lookups plus an LLM judge with a 300-entity human audit; planted fakes help partly.
Prior tested LongFact only, not paper reviews; the plan explicitly states the transfer gap to long-context reviews and unlookupable entities.
Same-item comparison against best cheap baseline with 0.05 margin and CI; but baselines are cheap, not a strong outputs-only method like a judge.
Not a sequential-chain problem; no dependency is removed, only independent work in phases.
